walkthroughs.body_html:
Internal Assessment: Investigative Study of a Religious Practice — a core area of Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Internal Assessment: Investigative Study of a Religious Practice brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Internal Assessment: Investigative Study of a Religious Practice.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Whose 1902 Gifford Lectures examined mystical experience?
options: William James
Rudolf Otto
Friedrich Schleiermacher
Mircea Eliade

mcqs.q: Which 16th-century Spanish mystic wrote Interior Castle?
options: John of the Cross
Teresa of Avila
Ignatius Loyola
Francisco Suarez

mcqs.q: How does Reform Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism?
options: The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.

Reform Judaism treats Jewish law (halakhah) as evolving and not strictly binding, embraces modernity, and grants gender equality; Orthodox Judaism holds halakhah as divinely given and binding in detail, with traditional practice maintained.
Reform Jews don't believe in God and Orthodox Jews do.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between act and rule utilitarianism?
options: Act utilitarianism judges each individual action by its consequences; rule utilitarianism follows rules that, if generally adopted, would produce the most good — sacrificing case-by-case calculation for predictability and fairness.
Act utilitarianism is about action movies and rule utilitarianism is about laws.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Act and rule utilitarianism are basically the same approach.

mcqs.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
options: The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Christians believe in three different gods.
